title: Impersonal Passive and Reporting Structures
summary: It is said that, He is said to be, and have something done: the impersonal reporting structures of research and news.

sections.heading: It is said that: the impersonal frame
sections.body:
When a claim is widely held but nobody in particular is to be credited with it, English uses an impersonal `it` with a passive reporting verb: `It is said that`, `It is believed that`, `It is thought that`, `It is reported that`, `It is estimated that`, `It is claimed that`, `It is widely accepted that`.

The `it` is a placeholder standing in for the that-clause and cannot be dropped, and the reporting verb must be passive. `Is believed that the site is Roman` has no subject at all, while `It says that the site is Roman` means that some document says so.

examples.right: It is believed that the settlement was abandoned after a fire.
examples.wrong: Is believed that the settlement was abandoned after a fire.

examples.right: It is estimated that the population of the city will double by 2040.
examples.note: The standard frame for a figure whose source is left unstated.

examples.right: It was once thought that the canals of Mars were artificial.
examples.note: The frame in the past, for a belief no longer held.

sections.heading: Raising the subject: He is said to be living abroad
sections.body:
The same content can be reorganised so that the subject of the that-clause becomes the subject of the reporting verb, with the rest reduced to an infinitive. `It is said that he lives abroad` becomes `He is said to live abroad`. Nothing is gained or lost in meaning; the second version is tighter, and it is the preferred shape in news writing and in abstracts.

The infinitive preserves the aspect of the original: a continuous becomes `to be living`, a passive becomes `to be built`. The usual error is to raise the subject but leave a finite verb behind, producing `He is said that lives abroad`.

examples.right: He is said to be living somewhere in Lisbon.
examples.wrong: He is said that is living somewhere in Lisbon.
examples.note: Once the subject has been raised, an infinitive must follow.

examples.right: The drug is known to cause drowsiness in some patients.
Three climbers were reported to be missing on the north face.
examples.note: Past reporting verb with a present infinitive: missing at the time of the report.

sections.heading: Earlier time: the perfect infinitive
sections.body:
If the reported event happened before the reporting, the infinitive becomes perfect: `to have caused`, `to have been destroyed`. `It is thought that a faulty heater caused the fire` therefore becomes `The fire is thought to have been caused by a faulty heater`.

The choice between `to have caused` and `to have been caused` is nothing more than the choice between active and passive, decided exactly as it would be in a finite clause. Ask whether the subject acted or was acted upon.

examples.right: The fire is thought to have been caused by a faulty heater.
examples.wrong: The fire is thought to have caused by a faulty heater.
examples.note: The fire caused nothing, so the infinitive has to be passive as well as perfect.

examples.right: The team is believed to have reached the summit shortly before dawn.
examples.note: Active perfect infinitive: the subject performed the action.

examples.right: Several paintings are believed to have been destroyed in the fire of 1834.
examples.note: Earlier time and passive together: `to have been` plus the participle.

sections.heading: The register of research summaries and news
sections.body:
These structures are the ordinary voice of abstracts, literature reviews and news reports, where a claim is relayed without being endorsed and without a source being named inside the sentence. `Smoking is now widely accepted to be the leading preventable cause of death` reports a consensus; `Smoking is the leading preventable cause of death` asserts it.

They are as much a hedging device as a passive. Used everywhere they sound evasive, and a claim the writer is willing to defend is better made directly. They are also the wrong choice when the source is known: if the study can be cited, cite it.

examples.right: Rising sea levels are widely expected to displace millions of people this century.
examples.note: Reports a consensus without claiming personal authority for it.

examples.right: The suspect is alleged to have falsified the accounts.
examples.note: `alleged` marks the claim as unproven, which is why reporting on legal cases relies on it.

examples.right: Chen (2019) found that the effect disappears in larger samples.
examples.note: With a known source, name it; `It is said that` would weaken the point.

sections.heading: Causative: have or get something done
sections.body:
`have something done` and `get something done` report that the subject arranged for someone else to do the work. `She had her thesis proofread` means a professional did the proofreading, not that she did it herself.

The word order is fixed — object, then past participle — and reversing it changes the meaning entirely: `She had proofread her thesis` is a past perfect and says she did the work. `get` is the more informal of the two and often implies effort or persuasion. Both also have an unlucky use in which nothing was arranged at all, as in `He had his wallet stolen`.

examples.right: She had her thesis proofread by a professional editor.
examples.wrong: She had proofread her thesis by a professional editor.
examples.note: Object before participle; the reversed order is a past perfect and means she did it.

examples.right: We are going to get the heating repaired before winter.
examples.wrong: We are going to get repair the heating before winter.
examples.note: `get` takes an object plus a past participle.

examples.right: He had his laptop stolen on the train.
examples.note: The unlucky causative: he arranged nothing but was affected by it.

sections.heading: It is considered that, not It considered
sections.body:
The reporting verb in this frame is always passive, so `be` is not optional. `It considered that the scheme is affordable` is missing `is`, and as written it claims that some unnamed `it` did the considering.

The slip is easiest to make when an adverb comes between the parts, as in `It is now widely considered that`. Whenever a sentence opens with `It` and a reporting participle, check that a form of `be` stands in front of the participle.

examples.right: It is considered that early intervention reduces long-term costs.
examples.wrong: It considered that early intervention reduces long-term costs.
examples.note: The frame requires `is` before the participle.

examples.right: It is now generally accepted that the two species are related.
examples.wrong: It now generally accepted that the two species are related.
examples.note: Adverbs sit between `is` and the participle; they do not replace `is`.

examples.right: The committee considered the proposal for two hours.
examples.note: With a real subject and a real object the active is correct; the frame is not always wanted.

slips: `Is believed that the site is Roman`. The frame needs its placeholder subject: `It is believed that`.
`He is said that he lives abroad`. Once the subject has been raised, an infinitive follows: `He is said to live abroad`.
`The fire is thought to have caused by a heater`. Earlier time plus passive needs `to have been caused`.
`It considered that` with no form of `be`. The reporting verb here is always passive: `It is considered that`.
`She had proofread her thesis by an editor` for `had her thesis proofread`. In the causative the object comes before the participle.
Hedging with `It is said that` when the source is known. If the study can be cited, cite it.

questions.prompt: ___ that the population of the city will double within twenty years.
questions.explain: The impersonal frame needs both the placeholder `it` and a passive verb. `It estimates` would mean that some named thing is doing the estimating.

questions.prompt: People believe the disease originated in bats. The disease ___ to have originated in bats.
questions.explain: Raising the subject out of the that-clause leaves a passive reporting verb followed by an infinitive.

questions.prompt: The fire is thought ___ by a faulty heater in the basement.
questions.explain: The event is earlier than the reporting, so the infinitive is perfect, and the fire was acted upon, so it is also passive. `to have caused` would say the fire caused something else.

questions.prompt: Rather than editing the manuscript herself, she ___ by a professional.
questions.explain: The causative puts the object before the past participle. `had proofread it` is a past perfect and would mean she did the work herself.

questions.prompt: The heating has failed again, so we are going to get it ___ before the weekend.
questions.explain: `get something done` takes a past participle, because the subject arranges the work rather than performing it.

questions.prompt: It is ___ that early intervention reduces long-term costs.
questions.explain: After `It is` the reporting verb appears as a past participle. `It is considering` would need a real subject capable of considering something.

questions.prompt: He is said ___ in Lisbon now that the trial has ended.
questions.explain: The raised infinitive keeps the aspect of the original clause, so a continuous `is living` becomes `to be living`.

questions.prompt: It has been reported ___ several villages are still cut off by the floods.
questions.explain: The impersonal frame with `it` is completed by a that-clause. An infinitive with `to` belongs to the raised version, which would begin `Several villages are reported to be`.

questions.prompt: Three climbers ___ to be missing on the north face, but all were later found safe.
questions.explain: The raised structure works with a past reporting verb too; the present infinitive shows the situation as it stood at the time of the report.

questions.prompt: Professor Lang ___ one of the leading authorities on medieval trade routes.
questions.explain: Once the subject has been raised to the front, the reporting verb is followed by an infinitive rather than by a finite clause.

questions.prompt: If you need the certificate translated, you should ___ it done by a sworn translator.
questions.explain: Both `have something done` and `get something done` report that the work is arranged rather than carried out by the subject.

questions.prompt: The expedition is believed ___ the summit shortly before dawn.
questions.explain: The expedition performed the action, so the perfect infinitive stays active. `to have been reached` would make the expedition the thing that was reached.
